Draft:
"Insulation slows heat transfer primarily by increasing thermal resistance and interrupting direct pathways. Heat moves via conduction, convection, and radiation. In conduction, rate is proportional to thermal conductivity and cross-sectional area, inversely to length: q = -k A dT/dx. Insulating materials use low-k solids or trapped low-k gas, raising k or adding thickness, so for same ΔT, smaller q flows.

Convection is suppressed by low-conductivity trapped air or fibrous mats that dampen fluid motion. Radiation can be reduced with reflective surfaces/low-emissivity coatings, though not eliminated. The overall thermal resistance model: R = ΔT / Q. Adding insulation increases R, lowering heat flow for a given temperature difference.

In practical GPU cooling, insulation-like layers (thermal pads, foam, PCB thickness, case gaskets) slow heat spreading into components or out of hot zones. But they don't stop heat; they slow transfer, raising temperatures until removed by cooling. Too much insulation can cause hot spots, reduce heat dissipation, or trap heat. General principle: lower thermal conductivity, reduced contact area/path length, and minimized convection/radiation aids slow heat transfer. The benefit is temporal—heat remains localized longer, useful for thermal throttling management or keeping components below thresholds, but ultimate steady-state heat removal depends on available cooling."
